# Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and ACM: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=secrets-certificates-q003 -->
### Question 1

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application reads the password of an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database from a configuration file on each instance. A new security rule requires that the password is rotated automatically every 30 days without a new deployment of the application. Minimal code changes are acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command every 30 days to change the database password, write it into the file on each instance, and restart the application.
- Store the password as a SecureString parameter in Parameter Store, turn on automatic rotation for the parameter, and read it at run time.
- Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager, turn on automatic rotation, and pass the current value to each instance as user data at launch.
- Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager, turn on automatic rotation, and change the application to read the secret at run time through a cache.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager, turn on automatic rotation, and change the application to read the secret at run time through a cache.

**Deciding phrases.** "rotated automatically every 30 days without a new deployment", "Minimal code changes are acceptable", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: the password sits in a file on each instance, it must rotate automatically every 30 days, nothing is redeployed, and minimal code changes are acceptable.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict Secrets Manager with automatic rotation and an application that reads the secret at run time, because a password in a file cannot change by itself.
4. I remove the SecureString option, because Parameter Store has no credential rotation to turn on. I remove the user data option, because a value read once at launch is old after the first rotation.
5. Between the Run Command job and the runtime read the difference is who does the work; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, so I choose the runtime read, which needs no job on each instance and no restart.
6. Check: Secrets Manager rotates the password, the application gets the new value when it next reads the secret, nothing is redeployed, and the code change is one SDK call with a cache. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Secrets Manager replaces a stored password with a [runtime call to the Secrets Manager service](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-runtime-call-replaces-hardcoded). Because the credentials are [no longer stored with the application](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-without-redeploy), a rotation needs no deployment. The code change is one SDK call, and [using a cache can reduce your costs](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cache-cost-latency) and latency. A cached value changes at the next refresh: for the Python caching client, [By default, the cache refreshes secrets every hour](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cache-refresh-hourly-default). After a failed login, the application reads the secret again.

**Why not.**

- "Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command every 30 ...": It can work, but the team runs and checks a job on every instance; a secret read at run time [no longer requires updating your applications](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-without-redeploy).
- "Store the password as a SecureString parameter in ...": There is no rotation setting to turn on: credential rotation in Parameter Store is [None](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-rotation-row).
- "Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager, turn ...": An instance that reads the value once at launch keeps the old password after a rotation; the application needs a [runtime call to the Secrets Manager service](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-runtime-call-replaces-hardcoded).

**Twin.** If the stem said "Amazon ECS tasks receive the password as an environment variable" instead: each rotation also needs new tasks, because [you must force a new deployment](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-ecs-redeploy-for-new-value).

**Takeaway.** To rotate without a redeployment, the application reads the secret from Secrets Manager at run time instead of from a file.

**Review.** [Secrets Manager replaces a stored password with a call at run time](2-deep.md#secrets-manager-replaces-a-stored-password-with-a-call-at-run-time-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application currently keeps one value in its source code. The value is a database password that company policy requires to be rotated automatically every 30 days. The company wants to move the value out of the code and read it at run time through the AWS SDK. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Store the value as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypt it with a new customer managed KMS key, and turn on automatic rotation.
- Store the value as a standard String parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and change the parameter value when required.
- Store the value as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager, and turn on automatic rotation.
- Store the value as an advanced SecureString parameter in Parameter Store, and attach a NoChangeNotification policy to the parameter.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the value as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager, and turn on automatic rotation.

**Deciding phrases.** "a database password that company policy requires to be rotated automatically every 30 days", "MOST cost-effective way"

**Why.** The value is a database password with an automatic rotation rule. Credential rotation is [None](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-rotation-row) in Parameter Store and [Automatic, with native database integrations](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-rotation-row) in Secrets Manager. The cheapest secret keeps the AWS managed key. The application reads the secret at run time, so rotation [no longer requires updating your applications](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-without-redeploy).

**Why not.**

- "Store the value as a secret in AWS ...": It rotates the password, but a customer managed key costs [$1/month](../facts/kms.md#kms-price-key-storage-per-month), while aws/secretsmanager is available [to encrypt your secrets for free](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-aws-managed-key-free).
- "Store the value as a standard String parameter ...": Credential rotation in Parameter Store is [None](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-rotation-row), so a person changes the password by hand, which breaks the automatic rotation rule.
- "Store the value as an advanced SecureString parameter ...": The [NoChangeNotification](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-nochange-notification) policy sends an event about an unchanged value; it changes nothing, and Parameter Store rotation is [None](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-rotation-row).

**Twin.** If the stem said "an application endpoint URL that the team updates by hand a few times each year" instead: a standard String parameter, because standard parameters have [no additional charge](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-price-advanced-parameter).

**Takeaway.** A password that rotates automatically goes into Secrets Manager; Parameter Store stores values but does not rotate them.

**Review.** [Parameter Store stores configuration and encrypted values but does not rotate them](2-deep.md#parameter-store-stores-configuration-and-encrypted-values-but-does-not-rotate-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company runs a web application behind an Application Load Balancer in the eu-west-1 Region. The load balancer has an HTTPS listener with a public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for app.example.com. Users around the world report slow page loads, so the company adds an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the load balancer. Viewers must reach the distribution at app.example.com, and data must stay encrypted in transit. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Select the existing ACM certificate from the eu-west-1 Region in the distribution settings, and keep it on the load balancer as well.
- Request a public certificate for app.example.com in ACM in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and associate it with the distribution.
- Copy the existing ACM certificate from the eu-west-1 Region to the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and associate the copy with the distribution.
- Buy a certificate from a third-party certificate authority, import it into ACM in US East (N. Virginia), and associate it with the distribution.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Request a public certificate for app.example.com in ACM in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and associate it with the distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "in the eu-west-1 Region", "adds an Amazon CloudFront distribution", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** CloudFront is the exception to the Regional rule. Its certificate is requested or imported in [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1) and then [distributed to all the geographic locations](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1) of the distribution. The load balancer keeps its eu-west-1 certificate, because a load balancer's certificate [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.

**Why not.**

- "Select the existing ACM certificate from the eu-west-1 ...": CloudFront reads its viewer certificate from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), not from the Region of the origin load balancer.
- "Copy the existing ACM certificate from the eu-west-1 ...": [Certificates in ACM are regional resources](../facts/acm.md#acm-certificates-regional), and [you cannot copy a certificate between regions](../facts/acm.md#acm-certificates-regional).
- "Buy a certificate from a third-party certificate authority, ...": It works, but ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for an imported certificate, so the team renews and reimports it by hand.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the company must keep its current third-party certificate authority" instead: import that certificate into ACM, still in [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1).

**Takeaway.** A CloudFront viewer certificate comes from ACM in US East (N. Virginia), whatever the Region of the origin.

**Review.** [ACM certificates are Regional and CloudFront reads them only from us-east-1](2-deep.md#acm-certificates-are-regional-and-cloudfront-reads-them-only-from-us-east-1-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company hosts its public domain in Amazon Route 53 and serves its main website from an Application Load Balancer. The company requests a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for the load balancer. The operations team wants ACM to renew the certificate automatically, with no action from a person at renewal time. How should the company validate the domain for this certificate?

- Choose email validation, and approve the validation email that ACM sends to the administrative addresses of the domain.
- Choose DNS validation, and add the CNAME record that ACM provides to the hosted zone in Route 53.
- Choose HTTP validation, and configure the load balancer to answer the validation requests that ACM sends.
- Import a certificate from a third-party certificate authority into ACM instead of requesting a public ACM certificate.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Choose DNS validation, and add the CNAME record that ACM provides to the hosted zone in Route 53.

**Deciding phrases.** "renew the certificate automatically", "no action from a person at renewal time"

**Why.** With DNS validation, ACM gives a CNAME record that is [added to your DNS database only once](../facts/acm.md#acm-dns-cname-records). ACM then [automatically renews DNS-validated certificates](../facts/acm.md#acm-dns-validation-recommended) while the certificate is in use and the record remains. The team adds the record once in its Route 53 hosted zone, and no person acts at renewal time.

**Why not.**

- "Choose email validation, and approve the validation email ...": Email-validated certificates [require an action by the domain owner](../facts/acm.md#acm-email-validation-needs-owner-action) at each renewal, so a person acts every time.
- "Choose HTTP validation, and configure the load balancer ...": HTTP validation is [only available through the CloudFront Distribution Tenants feature](../facts/acm.md#acm-http-validation-cloudfront-only), not for a certificate on a load balancer.
- "Import a certificate from a third-party certificate authority ...": ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for imported certificates, so a person renews and reimports it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the domain is hosted at another DNS provider" instead: DNS validation still works, because you [manually enter CNAME records provided by ACM](../facts/acm.md#acm-dns-without-route53) there.

**Takeaway.** DNS validation plus a CNAME record that stays in place lets ACM renew a certificate with no human action.

**Review.** [ACM renews a DNS-validated certificate while it is in use and its record remains](2-deep.md#acm-renews-a-dns-validated-certificate-while-it-is-in-use-and-its-record-remains-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application currently keeps one value in its source code. The value is an application endpoint URL that the team updates by hand a few times each year. The company wants to move the value out of the code and read it at run time through the AWS SDK. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Store the value as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypt it with a new customer managed KMS key, and turn on automatic rotation.
- Store the value as a standard String parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and change the parameter value when required.
- Store the value as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager, and turn on automatic rotation.
- Store the value as an advanced SecureString parameter in Parameter Store, and attach a NoChangeNotification policy to the parameter.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the value as a standard String parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and change the parameter value when required.

**Deciding phrases.** "an application endpoint URL that the team updates by hand a few times each year", "MOST cost-effective way"

**Why.** The value is plain configuration that people change by hand, so it needs no rotation and no notification. In the AWS comparison table, Parameter Store has its [standard tier free](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-cost-row), while Secrets Manager is [billed per secret per month](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-cost-row). The advanced tier and a customer managed key each add a charge that buys nothing here. The cheapest store that meets the need is a standard String parameter.

**Why not.**

- "Store the value as a secret in AWS ...": It costs more and does not fit: each secret is billed, a customer managed key costs [$1/month](../facts/kms.md#kms-price-key-storage-per-month), and rotation would replace a URL that people set by hand.
- "Store the value as a secret in AWS ...": It costs more and does not fit: Secrets Manager is [billed per secret per month](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-cost-row), and rotation would replace a URL that people set by hand.
- "Store the value as an advanced SecureString parameter ...": It works, but an advanced parameter costs [$0.05 per advanced parameter per month](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-price-advanced-parameter), and nothing in the stem needs a notification.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a database password that company policy requires to be rotated automatically every 30 days" instead: Secrets Manager, because credential rotation in Parameter Store is [None](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-rotation-row).

**Takeaway.** Plain configuration that people change by hand goes into a standard parameter, which has no additional charge.

**Review.** [Parameter Store stores configuration and encrypted values but does not rotate them](2-deep.md#parameter-store-stores-configuration-and-encrypted-values-but-does-not-rotate-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company stores a database secret in AWS Secrets Manager in account A. The secret is encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager. An AWS Lambda function in account B must read the secret. The IAM role of the function already allows secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret and kms:Decrypt on KMS keys in account A. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST securely? (Select TWO.)

- Add the IAM role of the function in account B to the key policy of the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager in account A.
- Change the KMS key of the secret to a customer managed key whose key policy allows the IAM role of the function in account B to decrypt.
- Attach a resource-based policy to the secret that allows all principals in account B to call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue.
- Attach a resource-based policy to the secret that allows the IAM role of the function in account B to call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue.
- Keep the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager, and add kms:Decrypt for account B to the resource-based policy of the secret.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Change the KMS key of the secret to a customer managed key whose key policy allows the IAM role of the function in account B to decrypt.
- Attach a resource-based policy to the secret that allows the IAM role of the function in account B to call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue.

**Deciding phrases.** "encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager", "Lambda function in account B", "MOST securely"

**Why.** Cross-account access needs an allow in [a resource policy and in an identity policy](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cross-account-needs-both-policies). The AWS managed key [does not allow any user to use](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-aws-managed-key-policy-fixed) it directly, so the secret moves to a customer managed key whose key policy names the role. Both policies name one role, which is the most secure scope.

- Across accounts the secret needs [a KMS key that you create](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cross-account-no-aws-managed-key), and [the key policy must give the external account permission](../facts/iam.md#iam-kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy).
- Cross-account reads need an allow in [a resource policy and in an identity policy](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cross-account-needs-both-policies); the role already holds the identity side.

**Why not.**

- "Add the IAM role of the function in ...": For the AWS managed key, [you cannot change the key policy](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-aws-managed-key-policy-fixed), so account B cannot be added to it.
- "Attach a resource-based policy to the secret that ...": With the new key it works, but then any principal in account B with an identity-based allow can read the secret.
- "Keep the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager, and add ...": A secret policy does not open a KMS key: cross-account access needs [a KMS key that you create](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cross-account-no-aws-managed-key) with its own key policy.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the secret is encrypted with a customer managed key whose key policy allows the role" instead: the resource-based policy is still needed, because cross-account reads need [a resource policy and in an identity policy](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cross-account-needs-both-policies).

**Takeaway.** Cross-account secret reads need a resource policy on the secret and a customer managed key that allows the other account.

**Review.** [Cross-account access to a secret needs a customer managed KMS key](2-deep.md#cross-account-access-to-a-secret-needs-a-customer-managed-kms-key-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company hosts an internet-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Scaling events replace the instances often. The company's domain is hosted in Amazon Route 53. Clients on the internet must connect over HTTPS so that data is encrypted in transit. The certificate for the domain must renew automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Request a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), and install it with its private key in the web server software on each instance.
- Issue an exportable public certificate in ACM, and run a script on each instance that installs the certificate after every renewal.
- Use a Network Load Balancer with TCP pass-through, and install self-signed certificates in the web server software on each instance.
- Request a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) with DNS validation, and add it to an HTTPS listener on the load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Request a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) with DNS validation, and add it to an HTTPS listener on the load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "behind an Application Load Balancer", "must renew automatically", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Ending TLS on the load balancer keeps the certificate off the instances: ACM is integrated with Elastic Load Balancing to [deploy ACM certificates on the load balancer](../facts/acm.md#acm-elb-deploys-on-load-balancer). With DNS validation, ACM [automatically renews DNS-validated certificates](../facts/acm.md#acm-dns-validation-recommended) while the certificate is in use and the record stays. New instances from a scaling event need no certificate.

**Why not.**

- "Request a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager ...": Associating an ACM certificate [directly with an Amazon EC2 instance](../facts/acm.md#acm-ec2-needs-nitro-enclave) [requires a Nitro Enclave](../facts/acm.md#acm-ec2-needs-nitro-enclave); a plain web server setup is not that.
- "Issue an exportable public certificate in ACM, and ...": It can work, but [you must manage the deployment process](../facts/acm.md#acm-exportable-you-deploy) on every instance, including each new instance after a scaling event.
- "Use a Network Load Balancer with TCP pass-through, ...": AWS lists [using self-signed certificates for public resources](../facts/acm.md#acm-wa-cert-anti-patterns) as an anti-pattern, and clients on the internet do not trust them.

**Twin.** If the stem said "users reach the application through Amazon CloudFront" instead: the viewer certificate goes into ACM in [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), and the listener keeps its own certificate.

**Takeaway.** For HTTPS to EC2 instances behind a load balancer, put the ACM certificate on the load balancer listener.

**Review.** [ACM certificates are Regional and CloudFront reads them only from us-east-1](2-deep.md#acm-certificates-are-regional-and-cloudfront-reads-them-only-from-us-east-1-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs an Amazon RDS for MySQL database in private subnets of a VPC. A custom AWS Lambda rotation function for an AWS Secrets Manager secret runs in the same private subnets so that it can reach the database. The subnets have no route to the internet, and every rotation fails because the function cannot reach Secrets Manager. The security team prefers private connectivity to AWS services. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST securely?

- Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet, and add a default route to the NAT gateway in the route tables of the private subnets.
- Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager, and add the endpoint route to the route tables of the private subnets.
- Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager in the VPC, and allow HTTPS from the security group of the function to the endpoint.
- Move the rotation function out of the VPC, and let it call the public Secrets Manager endpoint over the internet.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager in the VPC, and allow HTTPS from the security group of the function to the endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "no route to the internet", "private connectivity", "MOST securely"

**Why.** The rotation function has to reach both the database and Secrets Manager. In a VPC without internet access, AWS recommends [Secrets Manager service private endpoints within your VPC](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-private-vpc-use-endpoint). An interface endpoint keeps the calls private, because the traffic [does not leave the AWS network](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-interface-endpoint-privatelink). The function stays next to the database, and no internet path is added.

**Why not.**

- "Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet, ...": It works, but AWS warns about this path: [this exposes your VPC to more risk](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-nat-gateway-more-risk) than a private endpoint does.
- "Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager, ...": Gateway endpoints are [available only for AWS services including S3 and DynamoDB](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-endpoint-types-gateway-interface); for Secrets Manager, AWS recommends [Secrets Manager service private endpoints within your VPC](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-private-vpc-use-endpoint).
- "Move the rotation function out of the VPC, ...": Outside the VPC the function loses its path to the database; AWS recommends that the function [run in the same VPC](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-function-same-vpc) as the database.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the function must also write items to Amazon DynamoDB" instead: add a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB too, because gateway endpoints are [available only for AWS services including S3 and DynamoDB](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-endpoint-types-gateway-interface).

**Takeaway.** A rotation function in private subnets reaches Secrets Manager through an interface VPC endpoint, not a NAT gateway.

**Review.** [Automatic rotation changes the password on a schedule without a new deployment](2-deep.md#automatic-rotation-changes-the-password-on-a-schedule-without-a-new-deployment-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs an application in us-east-1 and keeps a warm standby copy in a second Region, us-west-2. The application reads its database credentials from a secret in AWS Secrets Manager in us-east-1, and the secret is rotated every 30 days. If us-east-1 fails, the standby application must still read the current credentials in us-west-2. The design must stay resilient, with rotation managed in one place. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function in us-west-2 that copies the secret value from us-east-1 into a separate secret after each rotation.
- Replicate the secret to us-west-2, and promote the replica secret to a standalone secret if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
- Configure the standby application in us-west-2 to call the Secrets Manager endpoint in us-east-1 to read the secret.
- Store the credentials as an advanced SecureString parameter in us-east-1, and share the parameter with us-west-2 through AWS RAM.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Replicate the secret to us-west-2, and promote the replica secret to a standalone secret if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.

**Deciding phrases.** "If us-east-1 fails", "rotation managed in one place", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Secrets Manager can [automatically replicate your secrets to multiple AWS Regions](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-replication-for-dr) for [resiliency or disaster recovery requirements](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-replication-for-dr). Secrets Manager [rotates the secret in the primary Region](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-propagates-to-replicas), and the new value reaches the replica. In a disaster you promote the replica [as a disaster recovery solution](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-promote-replica-for-dr).

**Why not.**

- "Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function in us-west-2 ...": It can work, but the team maintains copy code; with replication the rotated value [propagates to all of the associated replica secrets](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-propagates-to-replicas) without code.
- "Configure the standby application in us-west-2 to call ...": The call reads the secret [in the Region where the secret is stored](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-use-secret-cross-region-without-replication), so it fails together with us-east-1.
- "Store the credentials as an advanced SecureString parameter ...": Parameter Store [integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-sharing-advanced-ram) to share with other accounts, not Regions, and its credential rotation is [None](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-vs-secrets-manager-rotation-row).

**Twin.** If the stem said "both Regions stay up and the standby reads the secret during tests" instead: a cross-Region call works, because an application can use a secret [without replicating it](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-use-secret-cross-region-without-replication).

**Takeaway.** For a standby Region, replicate the secret: rotation stays on the primary, and you promote the replica in a disaster.

**Review.** [Automatic rotation changes the password on a schedule without a new deployment](2-deep.md#automatic-rotation-changes-the-password-on-a-schedule-without-a-new-deployment-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company runs internal microservices in several AWS accounts. To isolate its public key infrastructure, the company runs a private certificate authority (CA) in AWS Private CA in a separate security account and shares the CA with the workload accounts. Every client service trusts this CA. In one workload account, client services call an internal Application Load Balancer, and the traffic must be encrypted in transit. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Request a private certificate in ACM from the shared private CA, and add the certificate to an HTTPS listener on the internal load balancer.
- Issue a certificate from the shared private CA with the IssueCertificate API, import it into ACM, and add it to an HTTPS listener on the internal load balancer.
- Create a new private CA in the workload account, request a private certificate in ACM from the new CA, and add it to an HTTPS listener on the load balancer.
- Request a private certificate in ACM from the shared private CA, export it, and install it with its private key in the web server software on each target.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Request a private certificate in ACM from the shared private CA, and add the certificate to an HTTPS listener on the internal load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "shares the CA with the workload accounts", "Every client service trusts this CA", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** ACM can request a private certificate from [an existing private CA](../facts/acm.md#acm-private-needs-existing-private-ca), and the CA can be [shared with you by a different account](../facts/acm.md#acm-private-needs-existing-private-ca). On the HTTPS listener of the load balancer, ACM can [fully automate renewal and deployment](../facts/acm.md#acm-private-renewed-deploys-if-integrated) of the private certificate. The clients already trust the shared CA, so nothing changes on the clients.

**Why not.**

- "Issue a certificate from the shared private CA ...": It works, but ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for an imported certificate, and renewal of direct issuance is [manual (you call IssueCertificate again)](../facts/acm.md#acm-private-renewal-only-acm-issued).
- "Create a new private CA in the workload ...": ACM can use a CA [shared with you by a different account](../facts/acm.md#acm-private-needs-existing-private-ca); for a new CA [you pay a monthly fee](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-private-ca-monthly-fee), and an administrator [must explicitly configure applications to trust](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-public-vs-private-trust) its certificates.
- "Request a private certificate in ACM from the ...": It encrypts traffic from the load balancer to the targets, not from the clients to the load balancer, and [you are responsible for retrieving the new certificate](../facts/acm.md#acm-private-renewed-deploys-if-integrated) after each renewal.

**Twin.** If the stem said "external customers call a public load balancer" instead: a public ACM certificate, because applications and browsers [trust public certificates automatically by default](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-public-vs-private-trust).

**Takeaway.** For TLS between internal services, request an ACM private certificate from the shared private CA and attach it to the load balancer.

**Review.** [FAQ quick-fire](2-deep.md#faq-quick-fire-4-min)

</details>
